_about: Cross-cutting narrative for the explainer page (site/index.html, built by tools/build_site.py). Written from the September 2026 deep-read of the core papers and fact-checked against them; edit this file by hand to correct or extend it. Paper names here are display names, not data ids.
thesis: In 2025-26, most last-mile improvement of robot policies can be read as one loop: deploy, measure, find failures, improve, re-measure. The families mostly differ in which step they put effort into and which part of the system they change. Pretrained VLA and BC policies, once fine-tuned on a task, usually start well above zero, so in many recent papers the optimizer is not the main bottleneck. The bottlenecks are the signal (success checks, rewards, advantages, verifiers), trustworthy evaluation, and human and robot time. Many recipes that work keep the large model frozen and climb with something small: a noise vector, a residual or edit head, a critic, a verifier or a curated data slice. Others update the whole model but limit how far it moves: they restart each round from the pretrained checkpoint (RECAP), or keep the supervised loss and change only which data or advantage label it copies. Full-model RL with no KL anchor also works when the starting policy already succeeds often enough (SimpleVLA-RL). Under the new names, the classic ideas of perturb-and-score search and reward-weighted averaging are still there.

decision_guide.situation: You only have a scalar episode score (e.g. binary success), the policy is a frozen diffusion or flow model, and you want a cheap gain before trying RL.
decision_guide.use: Black-box random search or CEM over one fixed initial-noise vector (Golden Ticket).
decision_guide.why: The search space is tiny (28-1600 dims) and needs no log-probs. On a real Franka pick task, success went 80 -> 98% on 50 held-out episodes after 150 search episodes (~30 min). It can only select behavior the policy already has, so it is also the baseline any RL method should beat.

decision_guide.situation: You are tuning fewer than about 10 controller knobs (PID/LQR gains, impedance, MPC weights), and each real trial is expensive.
decision_guide.use: Bayesian optimization (GP surrogate plus MES for noisy objectives or LogEI for low-noise ones), starting from about d+4 initial points, the review's recommended default.
decision_guide.why: Of 110 hardware BO papers reviewed, 57 use vanilla BO, and the vast majority tune fewer than 10 parameters (Decade of BO for control). The authors place BO in the micro-data regime, where tens of experiments can be enough.

decision_guide.situation: A PPO or SAC policy has plateaued in simulation, and what you are graded on is a trajectory-level metric that does not split into per-step rewards.
decision_guide.use: A black-box 'stage 2' (SNES, TD-ES) that starts from the gradient-trained checkpoint and uses the exact metric as fitness.
decision_guide.why: EvolSAC cut cartpole swing-up time from 2.085 s to 1.135 s, where 1000 more SAC episodes reached only 1.565 s. TD-ES raised aggregate IQM success from 67.2% (PPO) to 85.0% on Isaac Lab Franka tasks (simulation only).

decision_guide.situation: You have a strong SFT VLA (roughly 10-90% success), a parallel simulator with cheap resets and an automatic success check, and 8x 80GB-class GPUs.
decision_guide.use: On-policy PPO with a critic, or GRPO/RLOO, anchored to the pretrained policy: low actor LR, a BC term, little or no entropy bonus, critic warm-up. For flow VLAs, use Flow-Noise/Flow-SDE or FPO-style ratios.
decision_guide.why: piRL took pi0 from 57.6% to 97.6% on few-shot LIBERO (sim, 8x H100). In the RLinf team's own same-codebase comparisons, PPO beat GRPO each time (piRL Flow-SDE: pi0 96.0 vs 90.0, pi0.5 97.9 vs 91.5; RLinf-VLA ManiSkill ID: OpenVLA 96.09 vs 84.38). ADEPT (sim PPO for a dexterous hand, not a VLA): standard PPO at LR 1e-3 got 0/5 seeds to ADR 50 (all collapsed at ADR 20), while the low-LR recipe got 5/5; adding a KL penalty did not prevent the collapse.

decision_guide.situation: The policy is at or near 0% on the target task.
decision_guide.use: Do not run plain RL or noise steering. Get successes first: prompt exploration (PDE), hindsight relabeling (LfH), human corrections or new demos, or change pretraining (TMRL).
decision_guide.why: With 0/1 reward and every rollout in a group failing, group-relative advantages (GRPO/RLOO) are exactly zero, and a critic sees no success to learn from. On one LIBERO-PRO task where action-noise PPO stayed at 0% for 120 steps, PDE reached 81.8% (the authors suggest that skills learned from successful exploratory rollouts on related tasks transferred). Noise steering cannot leave the base's support: from a 1-demo BC base at 33.5% on LIBERO-Long (zero-shot 0%), DSRL stays at 33.5 while MiDAS reaches 91.2.

decision_guide.situation: You are on a real robot with a budget of minutes to hours, and the VLA is too large or too costly to backpropagate RL through.
decision_guide.use: Off-policy RL around the frozen or co-trained VLA: an edit policy with argmax-Q selection over proposals (EXPO-FT, Real-Time EXPO-FT), or a small anchored actor on VLA features (RL Token).
decision_guide.why: EXPO-FT took pi0.5 from an average of 20.5/30 to 30/30 on 8 real tasks with an average of 19.1 min of online data. Real-Time EXPO-FT went from 42% to 97% on 4 dynamic tasks within a 10 min data cap.

decision_guide.situation: The base policy is roughly right but imprecise (alignment, contact, force, latency drift).
decision_guide.use: A bounded, zero-initialized additive residual trained with SAC or TD3: 50/50 demo/online replay, a LayerNorm critic on the summed action, and warm-up rollouts from the base policy.
decision_guide.why: ResFiT went from 14% to 64% on a real humanoid task after 134 rollouts (~15 min) and was about 200x more sample-efficient than a PPO residual on the sim BoxCleanup task. DAWN finds that seeding replay with base-policy transitions plus critic normalization (such as LayerNorm) fixes the critic cold-start and scale-mismatch problems that slow residual RL.

decision_guide.situation: The base policy already contains the right behavior but picks it unreliably, and you want to improve it in simulation without learning to exploit simulator bugs.
decision_guide.use: Latent-noise steering constrained to the base's support (DSRL, SCORE), or a hybrid of noise steering and a residual (RFS) when a mode switch and a small fix are both needed.
decision_guide.why: SCORE raised real success over 8 dexterous tasks from 37.8 to 89.9 with zero real-world RL, vs 59.5 for residual RL. RFS reports that noise-only and residual-only steering fail in opposite ways.

decision_guide.situation: You have success labels per episode and an existing SFT pipeline, and you want to learn from failures and corrections without RL infrastructure.
decision_guide.use: Advantage-weighted or advantage-conditioned BC: a value model, n-step advantages, and soft exponential weights or a binary advantage token with CFG. Restart each round from the base checkpoint.
decision_guide.why: Across 4 real bimanual tasks (20 trials each), Dissecting advantage-guided post-training found continuous weighting at 0.74 success vs 0.50 for hard filtering and 0.45 for DAgger (SFT 0.11). In RECAP's T-shirt/shorts comparison on the same data (read from the chart), RECAP on pi*0.6 reached about 60 successes/hr vs about 30/hr for AWR on pi0.6, at similar success rates (about 96% vs 91%).

decision_guide.situation: Your demos are mixed-quality or contradictory.
decision_guide.use: Curate before climbing: gradient-compatibility or influence scores (RoboDrop, CUPID, QoQ), or cheap smoothness filters.
decision_guide.why: RoboDrop raised average real success from 35.0% to 67.5% just by removing 17-21 of 90 episodes per task (each pool mixed 70 proficient and 20 non-expert demos).

decision_guide.situation: The policy fails in specific, repeatable places, and an operator can recognize and fix them.
decision_guide.use: HG-DAgger with correction reweighting and RaC rules (recover, then correct, then end the episode). Add robot gating or a learned intervention agent once watching time dominates. Switch to takeover-as-signal (RLIF, preference pairs) when the policy should beat the operator.
decision_guide.why: SOP: 3 h of wall-clock fleet interaction with human takeovers took the Base-1/2 model (pretrained on half of ~160 h of data) from 0.571 to 0.800, while 80 more hours of demos took it from 0.576 to 0.612. RaC reached 78.3% on shirt-hanging with 5 h of data.

decision_guide.situation: The policy is stochastic, pass@k is clearly above pass@1, and you cannot or will not retrain it.
decision_guide.use: Best-of-N with a verifier trained on your own evaluation rollouts (UF-OPS, SeeQ), gated so it runs only when samples disagree (VLA-ATTC), or one-step critic-gradient guidance (QGF).
decision_guide.why: UF-OPS raised the real ALOHA mean from about 38% to about 87% with best-of-10 (chart readings; the abstract reports an average 49% improvement over the base policy across 5 real tasks), using a verifier trained on 60 labeled evaluation rollouts per task. SeeQ took pi0.5 from 35.4% to 66.7% on real long-horizon tasks.

decision_guide.situation: Reward is a sparse success bit on a long multi-stage task.
decision_guide.use: A learned progress or value model used as potential-based shaping (gamma*Phi(s') - Phi(s)), not as raw reward, with a held-out ground-truth success check.
decision_guide.why: Robo-Dopamine drops from 85.0% to 41.3% without policy-invariant shaping. RynnValue: real DSRL averaged 72.5% vs 48.8% with sparse reward.

decision_guide.situation: You need to compare many checkpoints and real trials are slow and noisy.
decision_guide.use: A validated stand-in evaluator: a Gaussian-splat simulation rebuilt from a short video scan (PolaRiS) or a learned world model (Veo, RoboWorld). Check its ranking against 5-10 checkpoints with paired real trials before trusting it.
decision_guide.why: Veo eval: MMRV 0.03 and Pearson 0.88 across 8 policy checkpoints in nominal scenes (the paper reports 1600+ real trials in total). PolaRiS: average r = 0.9. RoboWorld: r = 0.989 with the RoboArena leaderboard (8 policies). Learned evaluators often get rankings right but absolute rates wrong.

decision_guide.situation: Real rollouts are the bottleneck, and you have a strong SFT policy plus an action-conditioned world model for your robot.
decision_guide.use: World-model RL or filtered BC on imagined rollouts: short branches from real states, refitting on the policy's own failures, reliability weighting.
decision_guide.why: RISE took real pi0.5 from 30-35% to 85-95% with no physical rollouts during the improvement loop (its world model and policy are trained on prior real demos and policy rollouts, and the policy also uses some human corrections). On LIBERO-Long (sim), VLA-MBPO shows full-horizon imagined rollouts falling below the SFT base (52.8 vs 54.6), while 2-chunk branches reach 66.8.

decision_guide.situation: You have a rough simulator of the task, 20-50 real demos and a pretrained VLA, and no budget for real-world RL.
decision_guide.use: BC-anchored sim PPO (sim-real co-training, then PPO plus a real-data BC loss). Then rebuild real failures as twins (F4R).
decision_guide.why: RL-Co took real pi0.5 from 45.9 (SFT co-training) to 66.2 with zero real RL. F4R raised real OOD success from 26.25% to 90.0%, vs 71.25% for budget-matched targeted BC. On one TacCoRL task (Assembly #2), sim RL with no anchor (beta=0) fell below co-training alone in real success (45% vs 55%).

decision_guide.situation: You pretrain a small actor-critic in simulation and can afford 10-60 minutes of on-robot training.
decision_guide.use: The recipe from “What Matters for Sim-to-Online RL”: keep or warm-start replay, update the actor once per 20 critic steps with actor LR 1e-5, and restore optimizer and target state. Optionally shape with the sim value (SGFT) or seed replay from a twin (TwinRL).
decision_guide.why: It reports near-perfect Franka vision grasping after about ten minutes of real training. A baseline updating the actor every critic step failed to improve on all robots.

timeline.name: SimpleVLA-RL
timeline.org: Tsinghua, Shanghai AI Lab et al.
timeline.note: DeepSeek-R1-style GRPO on binary success for a tokenized OpenVLA-OFT. LIBERO 91.0 -> 99.1; from one demo per task, 48.9 -> 96.9; a 0% start stays at 0.

timeline.name: Evolution Strategies at Scale (LLM)
timeline.org: Cognizant AI Lab, MIT, UCLA, UT Austin
timeline.note: Full-parameter ES with a population of 30. Countdown on Qwen-2.5-3B: ES 60.5 vs Dr.GRPO-v 43.8 at equal sample evaluations. Language only, no robot experiments.

timeline.name: ResFiT
timeline.org: Amazon FAR, Stanford, CMU, UC Berkeley
timeline.note: Off-policy per-step residual on a frozen ACT. Real humanoid WoollyBallPnP 14% -> 64% after 134 rollouts; about 200x more sample-efficient than a PPO residual on the sim BoxCleanup task.

timeline.name: VLAC
timeline.note: Pairwise progress critic trained on 4,000+ hours of video drives real PPO. Success goes from about 30% to about 90% within 200 real episodes.

timeline.name: piRL
timeline.org: RLinf team (Tsinghua, PKU, CASIA, CMU et al.)
timeline.note: PPO for flow VLAs via Flow-Noise and Flow-SDE likelihoods. Few-shot LIBERO (sim), pi0: 57.6% -> 97.6%; with Flow-SDE, PPO beats GRPO 96.0 vs 90.0.

timeline.name: RL-100
timeline.org: Shanghai Qi Zhi, SJTU, HKU, Tsinghua et al.
timeline.note: DPPO-style offline-then-online PPO on a small diffusion policy on real robots: 1000/1000 trials over 8 tasks, at about 14 h of robot time per task.

timeline.name: PLD (Probe, Learn, Distill)
timeline.org: NVIDIA GEAR, CMU, UC Berkeley, UT Austin
timeline.note: Residual SAC specialists on frozen VLAs generate recovery data that is distilled back. LIBERO (Spatial/Object/Goal average) OpenVLA-OFT 91.8 -> 99.2.

timeline.name: Ctrl-World
timeline.note: Controllable multi-view video world model. Success-filtered imagined rollouts lift pi0.5-DROID from 38.7% to 83.4% on novel instructions and objects.

timeline.name: pi*0.6 / RECAP
timeline.note: Value function plus advantage-conditioned supervised retraining plus human corrections. Laundry (T-shirts and shorts) ablation on the same data: about 60/hr and 96% vs AWR about 30/hr and 91% and PPO about 22/hr and 75% (chart readings; baselines start from pi0.6).

timeline.name: WMPO
timeline.note: GRPO inside a video world model refit on the policy's own rollouts, failures included. MimicGen (sim), 128-rollout budget: 33.6 -> 47.1, vs 33.2 for online GRPO on the same budget.

timeline.name: EGGROLL and TD-ES
timeline.note: On a single 8192-dim linear-layer benchmark on one GH200, low-rank ES reaches 91% of batch-inference throughput (PPO 34, OpenES 0.41). TD-ES as a stage 2 after PPO: IQM 67.2% -> 85.0% on Isaac Lab Franka tasks.

timeline.name: Veo world-sim evaluation and PolaRiS
timeline.org: Google DeepMind; UW, Princeton, Berkeley, Stanford et al.
timeline.note: Two validated evaluators. Veo: MMRV 0.03 and Pearson 0.88 vs real success for 8 policy checkpoints on nominal scenes (the report has 1600+ real trials overall). PolaRiS video-scan twin: average Pearson r = 0.9 across 6 unseen scenes.

timeline.name: SOP
timeline.note: Fleet-scale online HG-DAgger for pi0.5 (10 AgiBot G1s in the main run). Pretraining-scale ablation (half-data base): 3 h of on-policy interaction 0.571 -> 0.800 vs 80 more hours of demos 0.576 -> 0.612.

timeline.name: RL-Co
timeline.org: Tsinghua, HIT, PKU, CMU et al.
timeline.note: Sim RL (ReinFlow for pi0.5) plus a real-demo BC anchor for VLAs. Real pi0.5 average 45.9 (SFT co-training) -> 66.2 with zero real-robot RL.

timeline.name: RISE
timeline.org: CUHK, Kinetix AI, HKU et al.
timeline.note: Compositional video world model plus value model drive advantage-conditioned pi0.5 training; the improvement loop runs in imagination, but the models are trained on demos plus about 500-600 logged real policy rollouts per task. Real: 35->85%, 30->85%, 35->95% (20 trials each).

timeline.name: CoVer
timeline.note: Contrastive verifier picks among instruction rephrasings x sampled action chunks. SIMPLER red-team ID/OOD: frozen pi0 41.5/29.7 -> 57.0/61.0 with CoVer, beating pi0 fine-tuned on augmented instructions (44.0/48.7); stacking both gives 65.5/62.0.

timeline.name: Golden Ticket
timeline.note: Random search over one constant noise vector for a frozen generative policy. Real Franka pick 80 -> 98% on 50 held-out episodes after 150 search episodes.

timeline.name: Robometer
timeline.org: USC, UT Dallas, MIT, UW, Ai2, NVIDIA
timeline.note: General reward model trained with trajectory comparisons on over 1M trajectories. Real DSRL on a frozen pi0: 20% -> 85% in at most 45 min (10k steps), with 0 false-positive successes vs RoboReward's 45.

timeline.name: Simple Recipe Works
timeline.org: UT Austin, UCLA, NTU, Sony AI
timeline.note: Sequential GRPO with a rank-32 LoRA forgets little. LIBERO-Spatial AVG 81.2 with forgetting 0.3; full fine-tuning gives AVG 7.3 with forgetting 40.9.

timeline.name: Generalist GEN-1
timeline.note: Pretraining on 500k+ hours of wearable data, then about 1 h of robot data per task; learning from experience (RL) is named as an ingredient but not described. Reports 99% average on 3 charted tasks vs 64% for fine-tuned GEN-0.

timeline.name: EXPO-FT
timeline.note: Edit policy plus argmax-Q over pi0.5 proposals; the VLA itself is also updated with its original training loss, and humans intervene during training. 8 real tasks: SFT 20.5/30 -> 30/30 (HG-DAgger 22.1/30), with an average of 19.1 min of online robot data.

timeline.name: Siemens factory case study
timeline.note: A pure-SFT iterate-and-retrain loop on pi0.5 in a real factory, with recovery demos staged by teleoperating the robot into failure states (no on-policy interventions). 2,535 factory episodes plus about 900 in a lab mock cell. No final success rate given; the authors say it 'did not meet expectations'.

timeline.name: SCORE
timeline.note: Support-constrained flow steering of a frozen real-data policy, trained only in simulated reconstructions. Real success over 8 dexterous tasks 37.8 -> 89.9 (best baseline 59.5), with zero real-world RL.

timeline.name: ENPIRE
timeline.note: Coding agents run evolutionary keep-what-works search over training recipes on real robots. Going from 1 to 8 agent/robot pairs cut the time to near-perfect pin insertion from more than 1.5 h to about 40 min (an episode counts as a success if the task is completed within 8 retries).

timeline.name: Sunday ACT-2 Preview
timeline.note: Company-reported: 99.1% +/- 0.3% SE over 785 laundry attempts in unseen homes. The in- vs out-of-domain gap after the same post-training shrinks from 82 to 0 points with full pretraining (50 evals per point).

timeline.name: RoboWorld and DEED
timeline.note: RoboWorld neural evaluator: Pearson r = 0.989 vs the RoboArena leaderboard (8 policies). Separately, a low-budget RECAP-style adaptation on GR00T N1.6 (DEED) went from 32% (its fine-tuned DE policy) to 42% then 22% over two iterations (50 trials each).

timeline.name: Q-Planning
timeline.note: Frozen BC proposals plus a critic refit each round. Real stack-cups 40% -> 90% and insert-wallet 25% -> 80%; full-policy SFT on successes stalled at 55% and 30%.

timeline.name: Dyna: deployment is the eval
timeline.note: Fleet logging plus an SOP-step auto-labeler plus targeted retraining. Napkins went from 35/hr at 75% quality (Dyna-1) to 95/hr at 93% (Dyna-2); the post credits pretraining, model capabilities, tooling and systems together, with no ablation isolating the loop.

timeline.name: Dissecting advantage-guided post-training
timeline.note: Controlled real-robot ablation from one SFT checkpoint: SFT 0.11, DAgger 0.45, hard filter 0.50, continuous weighting 0.74.

timeline.name: Real-Time EXPO-FT, F4R, Decade of BO for control
timeline.note: Real-Time EXPO-FT: pi0.5 42% -> 97% on 4 dynamic tasks in 10 min. F4R failure-driven twins: real OOD 26.25% -> 90.0% (budget-matched Targeted BC 71.25%). Decade of BO for control counts 110 hardware BO papers.

lessons.lesson: These methods mostly select and amplify behavior the base policy already has. They rarely create competence from a zero-success start. Pick your method according to how often the base succeeds.
lessons.evidence: SimpleVLA-RL: an OpenVLA-OFT base with no task demos scores 0% on five RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and stays at 0% after RL. PDE: on a LIBERO-PRO task where action-noise PPO starts at 0%, action noise, Robometer and RND all stay at 0 for 120 steps; PDE reaches 81.8% by exploring with reworded prompts, whose successes on related tasks transfer. From a 1-demo BC base at 33.5% on LIBERO-Long (zero-shot 0%), noise steering (DSRL) stays at 33.5, while MiDAS, which trains a residual actor with value-based RL and reaches actions outside the base's effective support, gets to 91.2. The Golden Ticket paper notes its noise search works only if the frozen policy is steerable. Exceptions exist: ADEPT's RL learned a plate flip-and-regrasp the pretrained policy never succeeded at, and SimpleVLA-RL reports an emergent 'pushcut' strategy.

lessons.lesson: Freezing or tightly anchoring the big model and training something small is the safer default. Unanchored or aggressive full fine-tuning collapsed or forgot in several studies, though full-model RL can work when the base already succeeds often.
lessons.evidence: ADEPT (sim, Kuka-Allegro peg task): standard PPO at LR 1e-3 gets 0/5 seeds to ADR 50 (all collapse at ADR 20), while the low-LR recipe gets 5/5. PAC-ACT (sim, sparse-reward ablation): without its KL penalty between successive PPO updates, the policy drifts from the pretrained ACT's trajectories and the final training window drops to 72.7% (22.0% cumulative), vs 100% with it. Simple Recipe Works (continual VLA RL, LIBERO-Spatial): sequential GRPO with LoRA gives AVG 81.2 vs 7.3 with full fine-tuning. FlowDAgger keeps held-out skills at 0.88 (frozen base 0.96) vs 0.02 for SFT. TacCoRL (real Assembly #2): with no real-data anchor (beta=0) it reaches 45%, below co-training alone (55%); beta=0.1 or 1.0 reaches 80%. Counterpoint: SimpleVLA-RL updates all OpenVLA-OFT parameters with GRPO and no KL term and lifts the LIBERO average from 91.0 to 99.1.

lessons.lesson: The bottleneck has moved from the optimizer to the signal. Holding the learner fixed and changing only the reward, value or weighting often matters more than changing the algorithm.
lessons.evidence: SARM2: same residual RL from the same checkpoint (4/12 on Shorts Crumpled), and the reward source alone decides whether the loop climbs (SARM2 8/12), plateaus (Robometer-FT 5/12) or regresses (sparse 2/12). ViVa: 80.0% average real success with its value vs 63.3% with a VLM value in the same RECAP pipeline. Dissecting advantage-guided post-training: continuous advantage weights 0.74 vs hard filtering 0.50 mean success over 4 real bimanual tasks. RoboReward: in simulated Robomimic, offline reward accuracy correlates with RL success at r=0.83.

lessons.lesson: On real robots, off-policy methods that reuse every transition report far less robot time than on-policy methods. On-policy methods dominate where cheap parallel simulation exists.
lessons.evidence: ResFiT (sim BoxCleanup): 200k vs 40M steps against a PPO residual (about 200x), the only controlled comparison here. EXPO-FT: 30/30 on every task after an average of 19.1 min of online data, starting from a pi0.5 SFT policy. AutoSERL: 50/50 in 8-45 min from one demo (without start-position randomization). For scale only (different tasks and goals, not a controlled comparison): RL-100, which applies a PPO-style objective to iterated offline and then online rollouts, logged about 14 h of data collection per task (about 1.9 h demos, 6.8 h offline-RL rollouts, 5.3 h online), and FPO++ locomotion trains on roughly 147M-197M sim steps (4096 envs x 24 steps x 1500-2000 updates).

lessons.lesson: On-policy data, meaning the states the current policy actually reaches, beats more offline demos once imitation plateaus.
lessons.evidence: SOP: 3 h of on-policy interaction took a model from 0.571 to 0.800, while 80 extra hours of offline demos took it from 0.576 to 0.612. RL4VLA (sim): SFT plateaued at 0.781 in-distribution and PPO reached 0.938. PAC-ACT: doubling demos from 800 to 1600 moved BC only from 60% to 66% on Contour, where RL reached 100%. VT-Refine (visuo-tactile, evaluated in sim): going from 30 to 50 demos moved BC only from 0.48 to 0.57, while sim RL from the 30-demo policy reached 0.94; on the real robot, RL raised the visuo-tactile policy from 0.50 to 0.85.

lessons.lesson: A strong pattern: train on a convenient proxy first, then hill-climb the exact metric in a separate stage.
lessons.evidence: EvolSAC: SAC on a surrogate reward, then SNES directly on the target score. On the cartpole task, swing-up time fell from 2.085 s to 1.135 s, where 1000 more SAC episodes reached 1.565 s; the same recipe was then applied to the AI Olympics competition score. Q-Planning: on real stack-cups, critic-only rounds on a frozen BC policy go from 40% to 90%, where SFT on successful rollouts stalls at 55%. Related, but without a metric switch: TD-ES refines PPO checkpoints with bounded ES on the same return, lifting IQM success from 67.2% to 85.0% (Gaussian ES: 73.7%) at a fixed total budget.

lessons.lesson: Any learned judge (reward model, world model, preference loss) gets exploited under optimization. Use shaping, anchors, short horizons and an independent success check.
lessons.evidence: Robo-Dopamine: without its policy-invariant shaping, the raw progress reward drops a 3-task real average from 85.0% to 41.3%. FlowPRO: plain DPO on correction pairs collapses PACK success to 13% from an 80% SFT base. VLA-MBPO: full-horizon world-model rollouts compound model error and fall below SFT on LIBERO-Long (52.8 vs 54.6), while 2-chunk branched rollouts reach 66.8. PlayWorld: a policy fine-tuned inside a world model trained only on human demos peaked at 45% and then fell to 25% on carrot removal, below its 30% base (chart reading, 20 trials per checkpoint). GPT-5 as reward: in the SOLE-R1 authors' review of failed rollouts, 42% of failures come from hallucinated success, vs 9% for SOLE-R1.

lessons.lesson: Human time is the real budget. When and how a correction is collected changes results as much as how many corrections you collect.
lessons.evidence: TimelyDAgger (sim OpenDrawer) at a matched expert budget: 42% with immediate takeover vs 78% with takeover at step 80. UniIntervene vs HIL-SERL on 5 real tasks: intervention rate 14.6% vs 34.3%, success 88% vs 81%. PAKT reports 62%-86% fewer cumulative interventions than HIL-SERL. Skill-Space Shooting's machine corrector scored above duration-matched extra human demos on all 4 tasks: clearly on Coffee (71 vs 46 progress) and Sweeping (84 vs 63), narrowly on Stack-3 (0.83 vs 0.80) and Drawer (0.60 vs 0.50), one run each.

lessons.lesson: Average success hides regressions in speed, behavior modes, individual tasks and task handoffs. Report those too.
lessons.evidence: RECAP's ablation (laundry, T-shirts and shorts): AWR keeps about 91% success (RECAP about 96%) but about 30/hr vs about 60/hr. BMD (Avoid, 24 modes): residual RL keeps 0.98 success but solves only 1 of 24 modes at 80% or better, vs 20 for the pretrained policy. Uncertainty-gated exploration noise (one small-compute LIBERO-10 study with a 450M SmolVLA): PPO with fixed noise collapsed individual tasks in 2 of 3 seeds and learned noise in every seed, and no arm beat the BC baseline of 0.648. Foresight: residual RL lifts oracle-initialized subtasks to 98.4/92.2/99.2, but the chained full task stays at 54.5% (85.6% with foresight rewards). HELP: round-1 training on recovery data raised Test Tube success from 35% to 55% but slowed execution from 93 s to 105 s, as the policy made extra recovery moves (round 2 reached 95% at 93.4 s).

lessons.lesson: Small evaluations overstate gains near the ceiling. Separate search from evaluation and report confidence intervals.
lessons.evidence: EXPO-FT: 30/30 is still consistent with a true success rate of roughly 88-90% at 95% confidence. Golden Ticket: the SimplerEnv 63.0 -> 89.5 figure takes the best of 9 tickets by their held-out success (base numbers from NVIDIA's public evaluation), while picking by search reward gives +14.8 points. DEED's round-1 gain (32% -> 42%, 50 trials each) has overlapping 95% CIs, as the authors note, and round 2 fell to 22%. R2S-Eval notes that real-world success-rate rankings can change across repeated evaluations, and that policies with similar success rates can differ substantially in execution quality.

industry_recipes.recipe: pi*0.6 / RECAP. Deploy the VLA, have humans label every episode success or failure, and let teleoperators intervene (their actions are forced to 'positive'). Fit a distributional value on negative steps-to-success and compute n-step advantages (N=50). Binarize them into an 'Advantage: positive/negative' text token, retrain the whole flow VLA with its supervised loss (token dropped 30% of the time for CFG), and restart each round from the pretrained checkpoint. Also RL Token: a small TD3-style actor-critic on a compressed token from pi0.6 (task-fine-tuned on 1-10 h of demos, then frozen), penalized for straying from the VLA's own chunk.
industry_recipes.evidence: T-shirt folding, same data, different policy-extraction methods: RECAP about 60/hr and 96% vs AWR about 30/hr and 91% vs PPO about 22/hr and 75% (chart readings; AWR and PPO start from pi0.6, not the offline-RL pi*0.6 checkpoint). Espresso: about 40% after offline RL + SFT -> about 92% with RECAP (about 11% for pretrained pi0.6 with no task fine-tuning); the paper reports 13 hours straight of espresso making. RL Token: screw critical-phase success 20% -> 65%.
industry_recipes.disclosed: Algorithm, ablation and hyperparameters are published (arXiv 2511.14759). No code. Numbers are mostly bar-chart readings. The text's iteration gains (laundry +50% throughput, box assembly 2x after the second iteration) do not name their reference point, and Fig. 9 shows box assembly first dropping and then improving, so our readings against the initial policy (box about 10 -> 13/hr, laundry about 33 -> 60/hr) differ from them; treat these readings as approximate. The method relies on human labeling, interventions and resets, which the authors list as a limitation: the system is not fully autonomous.

industry_recipes.recipe: A learned video progress/reward model whose score dips when the robot makes a mistake acts as evaluator, failure finder and data filter. Flagged failure states direct targeted recovery-data collection, then retraining (human-in-the-loop active learning). At customer sites, 'deployment is the eval': fleet-wide logging (>1 TB/day), an auto-labeler that grades each SOP step against the customer's quality bar, human review of new tasks, ambiguous or low-confidence cases, suspected regressions and a sampled slice that checks label quality, and retraining on targeted slices. A separate hardware-health monitor keeps gripper wear from being mistaken for policy regression.
industry_recipes.evidence: DYNA-1: 850+ napkins in one 24h run with zero interventions at 99.4% success; Dyna reports 98% of folds at grade 3 or above and 75% at its production grade (4-5 of 5). Talk (Jason Ma, posted 2026-09-24): standard post-training stalls near 80%, and the reward-model loop reached 99.4% over 24 hours. Din Tai Fung: 35/hr at 75% quality (Dyna-1) -> 95/hr at 93% (Dyna-2). DYNA-1i: about 40 shirts/hour, 20 consecutive failure-free folds per 30-minute window in unseen venues.
industry_recipes.disclosed: No update rule, no reward-model accuracy, no RL objective and no ablation isolating the loop. Dyna credits Dyna-2 gains to pretraining, new capabilities, tooling and systems together. The talk's trial protocol (how many 24h runs stand behind 99.4%) is not stated in its public description.

industry_recipes.recipe: GEN-1: trained from scratch on 500k+ hours of human wearable interaction data with no robot data in pretraining, then about 1 hour of robot data per task. Five named ingredients: pretraining advances, post-training techniques, learning from experience (RL), multimodal human guidance and inference-time techniques.
industry_recipes.evidence: 99% average on three charted tasks vs 64% for fine-tuned GEN-0 and 19% for training from scratch without pretraining. Box folding in 12.1 s vs about 34 s for GEN-0 and pi0 (folding time only; baseline times taken from their earlier published sources).
industry_recipes.disclosed: Blog only; GEN-1 is offered to early-access partners. No algorithm details and no ablation of GEN-1's own components (the 19% baseline is a from-scratch GEN-0 with no pretraining). No trial counts behind the averages (only consecutive-success streaks, such as over 200 box folds in a row). The 64 -> 99 comparison bundles new pretraining, data, compute and algorithms, so the post does not show how much of it comes from RL.

industry_recipes.recipe: ACT-2: pretrain on sensorized human data from Sunday's proprietary capture hardware, then hill-climb reliability in-house on Memo robots. Run repeatedly, surface failures, post-train so the model learns from recoveries. Proposes the 'Solve' reporting standard: performance, declared scope, adaptation cost.
industry_recipes.evidence: Laundry: 99.1% +/- 0.3% SE over 785 attempts in unseen homes with one fixed checkpoint and no per-home adaptation. Generalization gap after identical post-training: 82 points with 0% pretraining, 0 with 100% (50 evals each).
industry_recipes.disclosed: The post-training update rule is undisclosed (deferred to an unpublished technical post). No ablation isolates how much of the 99.1% comes from the hill-climbing loop (the pretraining-scale study holds post-training fixed). Some garment categories have small samples (n=19, n=7).

industry_recipes.recipe: Helix logistics: no RL described. More in-domain demos plus architecture changes aimed at observed failures (stereo, vision memory, state history, force input, a 50% larger decoder).
industry_recipes.evidence: Over three months, barcode-orientation success went from about 70% to about 95% and handling time from about 5.0 s to 4.05 s. 10h -> 60h of demos: 6.84 s / 88.2% -> 4.31 s / 94.4%.
industry_recipes.disclosed: Blog only. Ablations appear in a figure with no trial counts or error bars. It serves as the demos-plus-architecture baseline that post-training loops must beat.

industry_recipes.recipe: A pure-SFT loop on pi0.5 via OpenPI in a real factory: teleoperate under constraints, hand-review every episode, re-fine-tune the base on all data, evaluate, collect targeted recovery demos, and relax constraints as a curriculum (a 70% gate per round).
industry_recipes.evidence: 2,535 factory episodes (about 10 h) plus about 900 lab episodes. Final success 'did not meet expectations'. In unconstrained trials, 65% of failed episodes left bag contents on the product.
industry_recipes.disclosed: A 5-page deployment case study with named root causes (wrist-camera angle, transparent bags, occlusion, contact). No overall success rate is reported.

industry_recipes.recipe: SOP: 10 robots run pi0.5, humans take over on failure, episodes stream to a cloud learner that publishes new weights every 25 steps (HG-DAgger or RECAP as the loss). LWD: a 16-robot fleet logs everything with sparse success labels, and a learner runs offline-to-online RL (distributional implicit value learning plus adjoint-matching policy extraction) over offline plus fleet data.
industry_recipes.evidence: SOP+HG-DAgger: Grocery 0.61 -> 0.94, Laundry 0.58 -> 0.96, Box Assembly 0.70 -> 0.98. LWD over 8 real tasks with about 60 fleet robot-hours: SFT 0.76 -> 0.95 (RECAP 0.85, HG-DAgger 0.85).
industry_recipes.disclosed: arXiv papers with methods. No public code for SOP was found (the project page listed in the paper returned 404 when checked in October 2026). LWD reports its 652.5-hour offline buffer and a roughly 60 robot-hour online budget, but not intervention counts or learner compute. SOP's Fig. 5 and text disagree on one number (0.895 vs 0.800).

industry_recipes.recipe: Physical Self-Play: competitive self-play RL in NVIDIA Isaac Sim (robot soccer; the post gives 'a single objective: score', and opponents are recent versions of the same policy), transferred to a real humanoid. Pitched as post-training to get past the ceiling of human-data pretraining.
industry_recipes.evidence: 140 simulated years of play, then a real humanoid match shown on video. No metrics.
industry_recipes.disclosed: No quantitative results, baselines or algorithm. On rewards, the post gives only the stated objective and says behaviors such as dribbling, shielding and tackling were not hand-rewarded. The post says 'a strong base model like S1' can learn this way but does not state how the soccer policy was initialized; it describes the policy as barely able to walk in its first simulated months.

industry_recipes.recipe: A learned action-conditioned video world model with a success-value head, used as a repeatable evaluator to rank checkpoints and architectures before real trials. The stated motivation: fully evaluating one humanoid checkpoint in real homes takes days to weeks and hundreds to thousands of trials, while the world model can replay identical starting conditions for every policy.
industry_recipes.evidence: A technical report states that a world model with 70% alignment picks the better of two checkpoints 15 points apart 90% of the time, and reports alignment rising from 63.06% to 71.17% with cross-task data. The 2024 challenge reports only token-level baselines (GENIE_138M at 8.79 CE loss on its GitHub leaderboard).
industry_recipes.disclosed: A blog plus a 12-page technical report. The report plots world-model scores next to real Arcade task scores for a few checkpoint sweeps and architecture pairs, but gives no trial counts or error bars for the real-world points and no correlation coefficient, and it does not show how the 70% / 15-point / 90% figure was derived.

classic_inside_modern:
Perturb-and-score search and reward-weighted averaging did not disappear. Most of it now runs as an inner loop inside newer systems.

1) Best-of-N with a verifier is one step of random search. You sample N candidates from the policy, score them and keep the argmax. This is the core of IDQL, V-GPS, UF-OPS, SeeQ, CoVer, RoboMonkey and TACO. EXPO-FT and Real-Time EXPO-FT use the same argmax over base and edited proposals, both for acting and inside the TD target (EMaQ-style). QT-Opt picks actions with CEM over a critic, and VLA-ATTC replaces argmax with a knockout tournament.

2) MPPI/PI2 exponential weighting shows up as 'softmax-Q-weighted averages'. Q-Planning executes a softmax-Q-weighted average of 32-64 proposal chunks, which is one MPPI step. SAILOR does MPPI residual search in a learned world model, and Simulator-in-the-loop cloth refinement runs MPPI in a GPU cloth simulator around the base plan. The Zero-order optimization primer shows MPPI is a natural-gradient step with step size 1/lambda, and that choosing exponential, rank or top-K weights gives MPPI, CMA-ES-like or CEM-like updates.

3) The KL-regularized closed form pi_ref * exp(A/beta) is reward-weighted regression, and PI2's weights are the same softmax. AWR, CRR, ARFM, IG-RFT and the soft exponential weights of Dissecting advantage-guided post-training use it directly. Filtered BC and rejection sampling (Hi-ORS, SOAR, RoboCat) are RWR with 0/1 weights. RECAP and CFGRL reach pi_ref * p(I|A)^w through an advantage token plus classifier-free guidance. QAM trains a flow toward pi_beta * exp(tau*Q).

4) ES-style fitness shaping appears in critic-free policy gradients. GRPO's group z-score, (R - mean)/std, is the same normalization ES at Scale applies to population rewards. ARS divides by return std, and OpenAI-ES and TD-ES use centered ranks. The difference is that GRPO perturbs actions per token or step and needs log-probs, while ES perturbs weights once per episode.

5) Noise-space search is black-box search with the generative policy as the decoder. Golden Ticket runs random search or CEM over one noise vector. Diffusion-ES mutates by re-noising and denoising. DSRL, SCORE, PSS and UniSteer replace search with an RL actor over the same noise space. PSS keeps only the top-k sensitive directions found by finite differences, and INSPO and SDN pick noise without training.

6) Black-box search at the outer level. ENPIRE runs evolutionary keep-what-works search over whole training recipes on real robots, similar in spirit to Eureka's evolutionary search over reward code, which it cites. Refinery uses a GP plus Bayesian optimization to pick PPO start states. VLA Grounder is compared against the evolutionary prompt optimizer GEPA. CMA-ES-IG learns user preferences from rankings. HandelBot's per-finger refinement is a non-learned, error-driven iterative correction applied before residual RL.

7) Black-box search as a second stage and for small knobs. EvolSAC runs SNES on the actor weights with the true competition score as fitness after SAC is trained on a shaped reward, and TD-ES continues from a PPO checkpoint with bounded-noise ES once policy-gradient gains become unreliable. BO remains common for small real-world tuning problems: of 110 hardware papers reviewed, 57 use vanilla BO, and most hardware examples tune fewer than 10 parameters (Decade of BO for control).

8) Shooting and tree search with world models and critics. GPC, IRASim, Latent Policy Steering and DreamSteer rank sampled chunks by predicted outcomes (random shooting). VLA-Reasoner runs MCTS with a frozen VLA as the prior. SVA runs MCTS offline in simulation and distills the returns into a critic that picks among frozen-VLA samples at deployment. tau0-VLA beam-searches over candidate subtasks, scored with a world model and a value model.

open_problems: Attribution in headline results: GEN-1, Sunday ACT-2 and Dyna-2 bundle new pretraining with the post-training loop, and none isolates the loop's share of the headline number (Sunday varies pretraining scale under a fixed post-training recipe, not the reverse). From the public posts alone, it is not possible to say how much of a 64 -> 99 or 75% -> 93% jump comes from hill climbing.

The 95-99% regime needs better measurement. With 30/30 successes, a 95% confidence interval still reaches down to about 88%; real-world success-rate rankings can change across repeated evaluations; many results are bar-chart readings or single seeds; and some papers change numbers across arXiv versions or reuse baseline rows from earlier papers. There is no shared, reset-realistic real-robot benchmark with matched budgets and confidence intervals.

No matched comparison across families: on-policy vs off-policy vs residual vs advantage-weighted BC vs test-time search vs world-model RL at equal human effort and robot time. Most papers compare against their own starting SFT policy or a few in-family baselines.

How far a policy can be optimized against a learned judge before the judge breaks: the 'No Free Checker' survey calls this question largely undeveloped in robotics and finds no shared benchmark for verifier exploitability, and hallucination detectors (HaWMPO, Sword) are only partial.

Starting from 0% without humans: PDE and LfH use large VLMs and are shown only in simulation or small real tests. Noise steering and search are capped by the base's support, and no simple test tells a practitioner in advance which regime they are in.

PPO vs GRPO and critic vs critic-free: three simulation comparisons favor PPO with a critic (RL4VLA; RLinf-VLA, 96.09 vs 84.38 on ManiSkill; piRL, 96.0 vs 90.0 on LIBERO; the last two come from the same RLinf team), yet widely used VLA recipes such as SimpleVLA-RL are critic-free GRPO. How this depends on policy type, reward density and budget is not understood.

Critic pretraining and anchoring: Cal-QL, ConRFT and FORCE say calibrated critic pretraining helps, while WSRL, IPE and Q2RL say naive pretraining adds little. It is also unknown how far bounded edits and L2-anchored actors can move from the base policy.

Regression and forgetting across rounds and tasks: DEED dropped from 42% to 22% in round 2; multi-task PPO collapses individual tasks (Uncertainty-gated exploration noise); one study finds that ES fine-tuning of LLMs causes significant forgetting, while a later analysis finds it need not; and only PLD shows a distillation flywheel back into the base at scale.

Objectives beyond success: recovery data can slow policies (HELP); in RECAP's policy-extraction ablation, AWR reaches 91% success at about half RECAP's throughput (about 30 vs 60 successes per hour, chart readings); and RL can collapse onto one behavior mode (BMD). Speed, quality and mode coverage are rarely optimized or reported together.

Removing the human: value-model and VLM interveners (UniIntervene, Skill-Space Shooting, AutoSERL, FIND) work on specific tasks. Whether they generalize, and what happens when they are confidently wrong, is untested. Most HITL results use one operator.

Contact, deformables and tactile sensing remain weak points for both video world models (contact hallucination per PolaRiS) and rigid-body twins. Sim success is only a partial proxy for checkpoint selection: F4R reports a sim-real success correlation of r = 0.7625 across 8 tasks and 24 checkpoints.

Whether weight-space ES (ES at Scale, EGGROLL) works on real VLA or diffusion robot policies, where episodes are stochastic and far more expensive than greedy LLM decoding. No robot results exist yet.

Perturb and score.classic: Finite differences, ES, CEM, CMA-ES, Bayesian optimization

Reward-weighted averaging.classic: RWR, PI² / MPPI, AWR. Filtered BC is the 0/1 version

Likelihood-ratio policy gradient.classic: REINFORCE → TRPO/GAE → PPO; GRPO group baselines

Bellman backups on replay.classic: Q-learning, DDPG/TD3, SAC, RLPD; chunk critics

Residual learning on a frozen base.classic: Residual RL, ResiP, Policy Decorator; noise steering

Reward shaping & learned judges.classic: Potential shaping, preferences, success classifiers, progress models

Model-based RL / Dyna.classic: Dyna, Dreamer, MBPO, action-conditioned video models

Domain randomization & twins.classic: DR + PPO, real-to-sim scans, BC-anchored sim RL
